questions.stem: A 33-year-old man presented with a 5-day history of loose stool and fever. He was known to have bronchiectasis and required frequent admissions to hospital for chest infections. He had most recently been discharged 2 weeks earlier. He had severe abdominal pain and distension and was passing mucus per rectum. Investigations: Peripheral white cell count 22.0 ×109/L Hemoglobin 14.2 g/dL C-reactive protein 156 mg/L Serum creatinine 195μmol/L He was admitted and isolated in a single room.
questions.lead_in: What is the next step in his management?
questions.explanation: Oral vancomycin This patent has Clostridioides difficile secondary to recurrent courses of antibiotics and hospital exposure, and he has markers of severity with his raised white cell count and serum creatinine. He should be started on therapy as soon as possible with oral vancomycin, which achieves high levels within the bowel lumen compared to systemic therapy. Imaging should be arranged to ensure he does not have toxic megacolon, requiring a surgical opinion and intervention. Imaging may show signs of toxic megacolon or bowel perforation in addition to bowel mucosa and submucosa edema. If lower GI endoscopy is performed to exclude other causes, pseudomembranes may be visible as raised patches of yellow and white, 2 cm in diameter, on the mucosa, but endoscopy carries a risk of perforation and should not be performed early on in disease.
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 5 Q19

questions.stem: A 64-year-old woman presented with a 5-day history of watery diarrhea without noticing any blood in her stool. She had not been experiencing fevers or chills. She had not had any recent international travel but had received a course of ciprofloxacin for a urinary tract infection 2 months ago. Investigations: Total white cell count 14.1 ×109/L eGFR >60 mL/min/1.73 m2 Stool Clostridioides difficile EIA for toxin A/B positive, GDH positive She responded well to treatment with oral vancomycin.
questions.lead_in: What follow up investigation is most appropriate?

options.text: EIA for toxin A/B and GDH
Stool culture for toxigenic C. difficile

questions.explanation: No follow-up necessary No follow-up testing should be done after successful completion of Clostridioides difficile infection. Detection of C. difficile toxins is possible even after successful completion of treatment but has no prognostic significance for recurrent disease.
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 6 Q27

questions.question: Fidaxomicin.

parts.text: Mechanism of action.
2 favourable pharmacodynamic qualities for fidaxomicin.
What is 1 clinical benefit of fidaxomicin?

cohort_answer.text: Inhibits RNA polymerase sigma subunit resulting in inhibition of protein synthesis and cell death; bactericidal. || Minimal systemic absorption – distribution mainly to GI tract; No dose adjustment needed for renal or hepatic impairment; Limited activity against bowel flora. || Decreased relapse rates compared to vanco/metro. questions.question: Patient who has a MRSA skin infection. And who has never had C. diff

parts.text: What is the most effective oral treatment that causes the least diarrhea in C. diff?
What is the most effective oral treatment that causes the most C. diff diarrhea?
What are two other factors in the treatment of this patient that have an impact on the development of C. diff diarrhea?
What are 2 antimicrobial measures to limit c diff risk?

cohort_answer.text:
Most effective oral treatment causing least diarrhea: Tetracyclines (also macrolides, narrow spectrum beta lactams)
Most effective oral treatment causing most C. diff diarrhea: Clindamycin
Two other factors: Advanced age; Duration of hospitalization; Prolonged exposure to antibiotics
Two antimicrobial measures to limit C diff risk: Minimize the frequency and duration of high-risk antibiotic therapy and the number of antibiotic agents prescribed, to reduce CDI risk (strong recommendation, moderate quality of evidence). Implement an antibiotic stewardship program (good practice recommendation). Antibiotics to be targeted should be based on the local epidemiology and the C. difficile strains present. Restriction of fluoroquinolones, clindamycin, and cephalosporins (except for surgical antibiotic prophylaxis) should be considered (strong recommendation, moderate quality of evidence). No evidence for d/c PPI or probiotics

questions.question: C difficile scenarios: 8mo old infant with non-severe diarrhea; 14yo M with second recurrence; 77yo F with first episode non-severe diarrhea; 50yo M with pseudomembranous colitis and developing ileus; 48yo M with second recurrence.

parts.text: For each scenario, state the appropriate management

questions.model_answer: a) 8-month-old, non-severe diarrhea: C. difficile toxin positivity is often not clinically significant in infants <1 year (high asymptomatic colonization); supportive care, treat only if severe/other causes excluded. b) 14yo, second recurrence: vancomycin tapered/pulsed regimen (or fidaxomicin), consider fecal microbiota transplant if further recurrence. c) 77yo F, first episode, non-severe: fidaxomicin 200 mg PO BID x10 days (preferred) or vancomycin 125 mg PO QID x10 days. d) 50yo M, pseudomembranous colitis with developing ileus (fulminant/complicated CDI): vancomycin 500 mg PO/per rectum QID plus IV metronidazole 500 mg q8h; urgent surgical consultation for possible colectomy. e) 48yo M, second recurrence: vancomycin tapered/pulsed regimen or fidaxomicin, with consideration of fecal microbiota transplant or bezlotoxumab adjunct.

parts.text: Describe the components of C. diff testing
What is the limitation to NAAT testing clinically?

questions.model_answer: a) Components of C. diff testing (multi-step algorithm): (1) Glutamate dehydrogenase (GDH) EIA - sensitive screening test detecting the common antigen (present in toxigenic and non-toxigenic strains). (2) Toxin A/B EIA - specific for active toxin production, confirms clinically significant disease. (3) NAAT/PCR (e.g. for tcdB gene) used to arbitrate discrepant GDH+/toxin- results (three-step algorithm), or clinical correlation with symptoms. b) Limitation of NAAT testing: NAAT detects the toxin gene, not active toxin production, so it cannot distinguish true infection from asymptomatic colonization - leading to overdiagnosis/overtreatment if used as a standalone test in patients tested without clear clinical indication.

questions.question: C diff: multi test algorithm explain, limitations to NAAT only testing.

parts.text: C diff: multi test algorithm explain, limitations to NAAT only testing.

questions.model_answer: Multi-test algorithm: begin with GDH EIA (sensitive screen for common antigen present in both toxigenic and non-toxigenic strains); if positive, follow with toxin A/B EIA (specific for active toxin, confirms disease); if GDH and toxin EIA results are discrepant (GDH+/toxin-), arbitrate with NAAT (e.g. PCR for tcdB) - this three-step approach improves both sensitivity and specificity compared to any single test. Limitation of NAAT alone: detects the toxin gene (potential for toxin production) rather than active toxin, so cannot differentiate true infection from asymptomatic colonization, risking overdiagnosis and unnecessary treatment when used as a standalone test.

questions.question: 16. A woman goes on an antibiotic for an infection, and later develops diarrhea. She is diagnosed with Clostridioides difficile diarrhea.

parts.text: What are two antimicrobial REGIMENS for this?
Which are the 3 lowest risk: Penicillins, cephalosporins, macrolides, clindamycin, tetracyclines, fluoroquinolones?
She goes on to have 2 recurrences: LIST 2 antimicrobial and 2 non-antimicrobial treatment options.

cohort_answer.text: Regimens: Vancomycin 125mg PO QID x10 days; Fidaxomicin 200mg PO BID x10 days. 3 lowest risk: Tetracyclines (OR 0.92), Penicillins (OR 2.71), macrolides (OR 2.65) [vs cephalosporins OR 5.68, fluoroquinolones OR 5.5, clindamycin OR 16.8]. Recurrence treatment: antimicrobial - fidaxomicin or vancomycin taper, rifaximin; non-antimicrobial - FMT or bezlotoxumab.

questions.question: Treatment of C. Diff (can only use a regimen once).

parts.text: 8 month old
13 year old with second recurrence
50 year old with fulminant colitis and ileus
40 year old with first non-severe episode

cohort_answer.text: 8 month old: ensure true C. diff (infants <12 months often colonized); if treated, can use same regimen as adults (vancomycin) with adjusted dose. 13yo second recurrence: strongest recommendation/evidence for fecal transplant; otherwise treated similarly to first recurrence (pulse/tapering vancomycin); option to use rifaximin for 20 days after initial vancomycin (fidaxomicin never gets a taper). 50yo fulminant colitis and ileus: Vancomycin PO + Metronidazole (Flagyl) IV. 40yo first non-severe episode: Vancomycin 125mg PO QID x10 days; Fidaxomicin 200mg BID x10 days; or metronidazole as a weak alternative x10 days at TID dosing.

questions.question: C difficile positive stool, agent and route (not dose or duration); can only use each regimen once.

parts.text: Baby with ongoing diarrhea
First occurrence, non-severe
Toxic megacolon
1st recurrence
Another 1st recurrence, can’t remember the subtlety, maybe one was a child?
2nd recurrence

questions.model_answer: Agent and route only (each regimen used once): a) Baby with ongoing diarrhea: supportive care only, no antibiotic (C. diff not treated as pathogen in infancy). b) First occurrence, non-severe: fidaxomicin, oral. c) Toxic megacolon: vancomycin, oral/per rectum (plus IV metronidazole). d) 1st recurrence: vancomycin, oral (tapered/pulsed regimen). e) Another 1st recurrence variant: bezlotoxumab, intravenous (adjunctive monoclonal antibody). f) 2nd recurrence: fecal microbiota transplant, per rectum/colonoscopic.

questions.question: C difficile

parts.text: Describe two tier testing and its rationale
Why may NAAT not be a great stand alone test?
List 3 intravenous antibiotics that can be dosed 3 times weekly with dialysis sessions

questions.model_answer: a) Two-tier testing: start with a sensitive screening test (GDH EIA, which detects the common antigen present in both toxigenic and non-toxigenic strains), followed by a specific confirmatory test (toxin A/B EIA) only if the screen is positive; rationale is that GDH alone is sensitive but not specific for toxigenic disease, while toxin EIA alone is specific but insensitive, so combining exploits the high negative predictive value of GDH with the specificity of toxin detection, improving overall accuracy and reducing overdiagnosis compared to NAAT alone. b) NAAT alone limitation: detects the toxin gene (tcdB), not active toxin expression, so cannot distinguish true CDI from asymptomatic carriage, leading to overdiagnosis and unnecessary treatment. c) Three IV antibiotics dosed thrice weekly post-dialysis: (1) Vancomycin (renally adjusted, given post-HD). (2) Ceftazidime. (3) Daptomycin (also cefazolin acceptable) - all commonly dosed after each dialysis session (3x/week) due to dialyzability/renal clearance.

questions.question: C. Diff

parts.text: Fill in chart: for Clinical Cure, Recurrence, and Mortality, state whether fidaxomicin or vancomycin is favored, or whether they are neutral (equivalent)
What class is fidaxomicin?
What is the site of action?

questions.model_answer: a) Clinical cure: neutral/equivalent between fidaxomicin and vancomycin. Recurrence: fidaxomicin favored (significantly lower recurrence rate). Mortality: neutral/equivalent (no significant difference demonstrated). b) Fidaxomicin class: macrocyclic (macrolide-related) antibiotic. c) Site of action: inhibits bacterial RNA polymerase (sigma subunit), blocking transcription - narrow-spectrum, minimally absorbed, sparing gut microbiota compared to vancomycin.

questions.question: Fidaxomicin vs Vancomycin for CDI.

parts.text: List if superior or equivalent: Mortality
List if superior or equivalent: Response to therapy
List if superior or equivalent: Recurrence
Fidaxomicin MOA
Fidaxomicin class

cohort_answer.text:
Mortality - equivalent. Response to therapy - equivalent. Recurrence - superior (fidaxomicin).
Fidaxomicin MOA: Inhibits RNA polymerase sigma subunit, resulting in inhibition of protein synthesis and cell death.
Fidaxomicin class: Macrocyclic class of antibiotics (Macrolide).

questions.question: Scenario with patient who develops diarrhea after taking PO antibiotics. EIA for Toxin A is negative.

parts.text: A) What are 2 other causes of antibiotic associated diarrhea
B) If the patient has C. diff, list 2 reasons why the initial testing was negative?
C) IPAC measures for preventing horizontal transmission of C. diff?

cohort_answer.text:
Post-infectious IBD: disruption of microbiota with antibiotics reduces carbohydrate digestion, reduces short chain fatty acid production - causes osmotic diarrhea - reduces bile acid breakdown - more diarrhea. Other enteric pathogens: disrupted normal flora allows overgrowth of organisms that induce diarrhea: C. diff, C perfringens, S aureus, Candida, K oxytoca, Salmonella. Direct effect of antibiotic: occurs in 5-30% of pts on antibiotics (RF: age>65, immunosuppressed, ICU, prolonged hospitalization); AmoxClav can stimulate bowel motility; Erythromycin causes accelerated gastric emptying; Penicillins cause segmental colitis
Variant of toxin B that produces Toxin B only; Low level toxin production below threshold of EIA Detection; Delay between stool collection and delivery to lab – toxin degrades at room temp and may be undetectable within 2h (should be stored at 4C if delay in transport)
Isolation: Private room with dedicated toilet; Contact precautions until 48h after diarrhea resolved. HCW: contact precautions, hand hygiene (soap + water preferred). Patients: encourage hand hygiene. Equipment: Disposable equipment or thoroughly disinfect with sporicidal agent. Room cleaning: terminal room clean with sporicidal agent, daily cleaning with sporicidal agent. ASP

questions.question: C. Diff

parts.text: A. Four strategies that can be implemented by infection prevention & control to control spread of C. difficile in institutions.

cohort_answer.text: Contact isolation with private toilet for known or suspected cases; Hand hygiene soap and water for visible soiling; Daily and Terminal sporicidal cleaning of pt room; Use antibiotics judiciously; Surveillance

questions.question: C diff

parts.text: A. Name two factors that make NAP-1 strain of C. diff hypervirulent. (North American pulsed-field gel electrophoresis type 1)
B. Name four infection control measures

cohort_answer.text:
Hyperexpression of Toxin A and Toxin B; Binary toxin (CDT) - increased toxin adhesion and uptake; Hypersporulation
Contact isolation with private toilet for known or suspected cases; Hand hygiene with soap and water; Daily and Terminal sporicidal cleaning of pt room; Use antibiotics judiciously; Surveillance

parts.text: A) Name 2 factors that make the NAP-1 strain of C. diff hypervirulent?

cohort_answer.text: Increased production of toxin A and B; Produces binary toxin (leads to increased bacterial adhesion, higher mortality); Resistant to FQ; Hypersporulation (more spread). [Background: resistant to newer fluoroquinolones, harbor tcdC mutation causing frameshift/truncated nonfunctional protein]

parts.text: Name 4 infection prevention and control measures

cohort_answer.text: Private room; Single-use equipment where possible; Contact precautions; Hand hygiene; Bleach for cleaning ("sporicidal"); Terminal cleaning

parts.text: Management of a patient with severe C. difficile colitis.

cohort_answer.text: For initial episode of severe disease: Vancomycin 125mg orally 4 times daily for 10 days, or Fidaxomicin 200mg orally twice daily for 10 days. For initial episode of fulminant disease: Vancomycin 500mg orally or by NG tube 4x daily plus Metronidazole 500mg IV q8h. Consider rectal vancomycin instillation if complete ileus.

questions.question: C difficile treatment scenarios (do not use same regimen for each): 8 month old with chronic diarrhea; 13M with second recurrence; 50yo with fevers, ileus, shock; 45yo with second recurrence

parts.text: 8 month old with chronic diarrhea - treatment
13M with second recurrence - treatment
50yo with fevers, ileus, shock - treatment
45yo with second recurrence - treatment

cohort_answer.text: 8 month old: No treatment indicated unless other causes ruled out; if treating, Metronidazole 30mg/kg/day in 4 doses for 10-14 days. 13M second recurrence: Vancomycin 125mg PO QID x10 days or tapered. 50yo fevers/ileus/shock (fulminant): Vancomycin 500mg PO QID + Metronidazole 500mg IV Q8 + rectal instillation of vancomycin. 45yo second recurrence: Fidaxomicin 200mg PO BID x10 days OR Vancomycin 125mg PO QID x10 days followed by prolonged taper OR Vancomycin 125mg PO QID x10 days followed by rifaximin 400mg TID x20 days.

questions.question: C difficile

parts.text: Describe two tier testing and its rationale
Why may NAAT not be a great stand alone test?

cohort_answer.text: Step 1 - testing for both glutamate dehydrogenase antigen (found on all C difficile isolates) and toxin A/B using enzyme linked immunoassay: GDH - high sensitivity, lower specificity; Toxins - high specificity, low sensitivity. Step 2 - NAAT testing to confirm presence of C diff toxin gene specific to toxigenic strains (highly sensitive so can rule out infection if negative but does not discriminate between toxin producing and non-toxin producing, colonizing C difficile). Want NAAT testing to follow up if discordant results between GDH and toxin antigens - more expensive but more specific for toxigenic strains, and sensitive

questions.question: C difficile. Do not use same regimen (antibiotic regimens).

parts.text: 8 month old with chronic diarrhea.
13M with second recurrence.
50 year old with fevers, ileus, shock.
45 year old with second recurrence.

cohort_answer.text:
8 month old: No treatment indicated (should not test in those <2, as routine colonizer that doesn't cause disease). [Note: less toxin receptors in neonatal colons, maternal Ab, different microbiome.]
13M second recurrence: Vancomycin 40mg/kg/day in 4 divided doses (10mg/kg/dose, max 125mg/dose) x10-14 days, then 10mg/kg/dose BID x7 days, then 10mg/kg/dose once daily x7 days, then 10mg/kg/dose q2-3 days x2-8 weeks.
50yo fevers, ileus, shock: Vancomycin 500mg PO/NG QID + Metronidazole 500mg IV q8h + rectal instillation of vancomycin (if ileus present).
45yo second recurrence: Vancomycin 125mg PO qid x10 days followed by Rifaximin 400mg TID x20 days; OR Vancomycin 125mg PO qid x10-14 days, then BID x7 days, then once daily x7 days, then 125mg PO q2-3 days x2-8 weeks; OR Fidaxomicin 200mg BID x10 days; OR Fidaxomicin 200mg BID x5 days then 200mg PO EOD x20 days; OR Fecal Microbiota Transplantation.
